open class AlphaComplexDQPStream(val points: Array[Array[Double]], val alphaComplexDQP: AlphaComplexDQP) extends AlphaShapes

Wraps an ALREADY-BUILT AlphaComplexDQP (any space/maxPower/maxDimension, e.g. AlphaComplexDQP.dtm's DTM-weighted output, or a radius-truncated .weighted/.euclidean call) as an AlphaShapes stream -- the exact same iterateDimension/filtrationOrdering/filtrationValue shape AlphaShapeDQP uses for its own always-untruncated, always-unweighted build, just parameterized over a caller-supplied one instead of building a fresh untruncated AlphaComplexDQP.euclidean internally. points is needed only to satisfy AlphaShapes's own metricSpace contract (unused by homology engines, see that trait's doc); it must be the SAME points alphaComplexDQP was built from.

final case class AlphaDQPSettings(rankTolerance: Double = ..., feasibilityTolerance: Double = ..., zeroTolerance: Double = ..., equalityTolerance: Double = ..., maxIterationsPerQP: Int = ..., workingSetCapacity: Int = ..., enforceMonotonicity: Boolean = ..., parallel: Boolean = ..., verbose: Boolean = ..., rescueRankTolerance: Double = ...)

Settings of the quadratic programs. All tolerances are relative, so they survive rescaling the points.

Settings of the quadratic programs. All tolerances are relative, so they survive rescaling the points.

Value parameters

enforceMonotonicity

make each value at least the largest of its facets', and equal to it within solver accuracy (see clampMonotone): the values are monotone mathematically, and the persistence algorithms need it exactly.

equalityTolerance

consistency threshold for dependent equality constraints (relative to max|U|).

feasibilityTolerance

a constraint counts as violated when its slack exceeds this fraction of max|U|.

maxIterationsPerQP

iteration cap per QP; 0 means 20n + 200.

parallel

run the per-vertex loop on the common ForkJoinPool. Output is deterministic. Default: on, where there are threads to share the work (the JVM; a Scala.js program has one).

rankTolerance

a constraint counts as linearly dependent on the working set when its Schur complement falls below this fraction of B_jj. Values between 1e-7 and 1e-5 work; smaller lets nearly singular factorizations through (non-convergence or wrong answers), larger rejects real directions. A candidate ruled out for this reason gets a second attempt (rescueRankTolerance).

rescueRankTolerance

a candidate that rankTolerance rules out because of a small pivot is solved again with this smaller tolerance and kept if the multipliers it ends with satisfy the optimality conditions of the dual against the data. In high ambient dimension many valid simplices are that ill-conditioned. 0 turns the second attempt off.

verbose

print a line to stderr whenever a candidate is left out because its QP did not converge.

workingSetCapacity

max active set size; 0 means "ambient dimension + 2", which is a hard bound since the active rows live in R^m. Raise it only if you hit the corresponding exception.

zeroTolerance

threshold on multipliers in the ratio tests.

object BarcodeDistance

Bottleneck and Wasserstein distances between persistence diagrams, by bipartite matching where each point may also be matched to its projection on the diagonal.

Bottleneck and Wasserstein distances between persistence diagrams, by bipartite matching where each point may also be matched to its projection on the diagonal.

The parameters follow GUDHI and Hera: groundNorm (their internal_p) measures one matched pair in the birth-death plane; order (their order, q in Kerber-Morozov-Nigmetov 2017) is the exponent the costs of all pairs are combined with. Wasserstein distance tends to bottleneck distance as order -> Infinity; use bottleneckDistance for that case.

'''Essential bars''' are matched only to essential bars, in order of birth (which is optimal for both distances). If the diagrams have different numbers of essential bars, the distance is Infinity.

object BinaryIO

Shared little-endian binary primitives for the binary file formats this package reads/writes (Ripser's packed distance-matrix format, DIPHA's binary container format). Every such format is little-endian on disk regardless of host byte order -- confirmed directly against both projects' own source (Ripser's read reverses bytes only if (is_big_endian), i.e. the file itself is always little-endian; DIPHA's own README states "little-endian binary format" outright) -- so ByteBuffer.order(LITTLE_ENDIAN) is used unconditionally here rather than detecting host order, matching both.

object BlockParallelReduction

An experiment (JVM only, #192): persistent cohomology of a Vietoris-Rips complex over F_p, degree by degree with clearing as Ripser does (degree 0 by union-find), on explicit coboundary matrices, reduced either sequentially or by edge blocks on a thread pool. Both reductions run the same column arithmetic on the same matrices.

An experiment (JVM only, #192): persistent cohomology of a Vietoris-Rips complex over F_p, degree by degree with clearing as Ripser does (degree 0 by union-find), on explicit coboundary matrices, reduced either sequentially or by edge blocks on a thread pool. Both reductions run the same column arithmetic on the same matrices.

Cells are ordered by block (a cell's first longest edge, by length, then smaller end, then larger end), then dimension, then the layered generator's order. A coface's block is never before its face's, so a column's entries lie in its own block or later ones, and only columns of the same block can have their pivot inside it. Phase 1 reduces each block's columns (in reverse order, as cohomology goes) by that block's columns only, while the pivot stays in the block: every pair it makes is one the sequential reduction makes. A column whose pivot leaves its block is deferred. Phase 2a reduces the deferred columns, in parallel, by the columns phase 1 paired (final, so only read); phase 2b finishes them one by one in order. A positive chunk merges consecutive blocks into units of at least that many columns, which is the chunk algorithm of Bauer, Kerber and Reininghaus with chunk boundaries on block boundaries (all the argument needs is that a unit is contiguous in the order).

java -cp $CP org.appliedtopology.tda4j.BlockParallelReduction      [trials] [seed] [p]

dataset is cube (uniform in the unit cube of R^d), torus or sphere (in R^3, with noise), or alpha: for the cloud's alpha complex instead (blocks by filtration value, fromStream; threshold ignored); method is seq, blocks-, chunks--, packed (PackedRipserCohomologyEngine, pairs only), packed-cocycles, verb (alpha: AlphaShapes, then Persistence), check (every method agrees) or dump (the points as CSV, for C++ Ripser). Each run builds the matrices once and reduces trials times; times are medians.

object BootstrapBand

A resampling confidence band for the bars of one degree, after Fasy, Lecci, Rinaldo, Wasserman, Balakrishnan and Singh, "Confidence sets for persistence diagrams" (Annals of Statistics 42, 2014).

A resampling confidence band for the bars of one degree, after Fasy, Lecci, Rinaldo, Wasserman, Balakrishnan and Singh, "Confidence sets for persistence diagrams" (Annals of Statistics 42, 2014).

Compute the diagram of the points, then of many resamples of them, and measure how far (in bottleneck distance) each resample's diagram is from the original. The 1 - alpha quantile of those distances is the band's width: a resample moves the diagram by at most width in 1 - alpha of the draws. A bar that persists longer than 2 * width cannot be matched to the diagonal by a perturbation of that size, so it is a feature that survives the resampling; a bar shorter than that could be one of the noise. Band.threshold is 2 * width, and diagram.longerThan(band.threshold) keeps the bars beyond it.

This is a resampling heuristic with a statistical reading, not a proof: the guarantee of the paper is for specific estimators and sampling models. Resampling with replacement (Resampling.Bootstrap) follows the paper's recipe. Resampling.Subsample draws fewer points without replacement and is cheaper; its distances are not rescaled to the full sample, so its band is wider than the bootstrap's (the conservative direction). Essential bars are left out of the comparison, so the band says nothing about them.

open class BowyerWatsonDelaunay(pts: Array[Array[Double]], seed: Long = ...)(using factor: EpsilonFactor) extends DelaunayAlphaShapes

The Delaunay triangulation of a point cloud by Bowyer–Watson insertion, filtered as an alpha complex: for point clouds in 2 to 4 dimensions (of their affine span), the fast way to the whole alpha complex.

The Delaunay triangulation of a point cloud by Bowyer–Watson insertion, filtered as an alpha complex: for point clouds in 2 to 4 dimensions (of their affine span), the fast way to the whole alpha complex.

Points are inserted one at a time in a randomized, spatially sorted order; each insertion removes the simplices whose circumspheres contain the new point and fills the hole with simplices through it. The hull is handled with a vertex at infinity. Every geometric decision is exact (DelaunayPredicates), and points exactly on a circumsphere are decided by a perturbation that depends only on the points' order in the input, so the result is a valid triangulation for any input, degenerate ones (grids, cospherical points) included, and the same for every seed. Points that coincide exactly with an earlier one are joined to it by an edge of value 0.

Value parameters

pts

the points; their affine span must have dimension 1 to 4

seed

seeds the insertion order, which affects only the running time

open class BowyerWatsonTriangulation(coordinates: Array[Array[Double]], seed: Long, checkEveryStep: Boolean = ...)

The triangulation behind BowyerWatsonDelaunay, on flat arrays: cell c has vertices vertex(c, 0 .. d) and, for each position i, the neighbouring cell across the facet opposite vertex(c, i). Finite cells are positively oriented. The vertex at infinity is the index n; a cell containing it (an "infinite" cell, one per hull facet) is stored so that replacing the vertex at infinity by a point beyond its hull facet gives a positive orientation, which makes "copy the cell and put the new point where the removed vertex was" correct for every cell.

open class CellularCohomologyEngine[CellT, CoefficientT, FiltrationT](val packSimplices: Boolean = ..., val useUnionFind: Boolean = ...)(using evidence$1: OrderedCell { type Self = CellT; }, evidence$2: Field { type Self = CoefficientT; }, evidence$3: Ordering[FiltrationT])

Persistent cohomology for any cell type (simplices, cubes, simplicial-set generators): the reduction of the coboundary matrix, following Bauer's Ripser (arXiv:1908.02518) without its Vietoris-Rips-specific shortcuts. Over a field the barcode is the same as the homology barcode; what this engine adds is cocycle representatives, and it works where the Ripser engines do not (Cech, alpha, cubical, simplicial sets, non-flag complexes).

Persistent cohomology for any cell type (simplices, cubes, simplicial-set generators): the reduction of the coboundary matrix, following Bauer's Ripser (arXiv:1908.02518) without its Vietoris-Rips-specific shortcuts. Over a field the barcode is the same as the homology barcode; what this engine adds is cocycle representatives, and it works where the Ripser engines do not (Cech, alpha, cubical, simplicial sets, non-flag complexes).

The coboundary is built by inverting the boundaries of the stream's cells, so the stream is read in full first. There is no maxDim: the stream decides the top degree. For degrees 0 .. k, pass a stream with cells up to dimension k + 1 (LimitedCofaceSimplexStream(stream, k + 1) for a coface stream) and ignore the degree-(k + 1) bars.

Representatives: every bar carries its V-column. For an essential bar it is a cocycle of the whole complex; for a finite bar its coboundary is the bar's reduced column, which is born at or after the bar's death, so it is a cocycle on the subcomplex before the death. coboundaryOfChain checks either.

Simplices with Int vertices (every complex the library builds: alpha, Čech, witness, Dowker, explicit streams) are reduced on flat arrays: each dimension's vertex tuples, a table from a tuple to its cell (the vertices side by side in one Long when they fit, else a hash of them), and each coboundary block as compressed columns of signs. Only a column that needs an addition becomes a Chain, and only the cells of the representatives returned are looked up again. The bars and representatives are exactly those of reducing the cells themselves.

Degree 0 is paired by union-find over the edges (the elder rule) when every edge is c·(v - u) between two cells of the stream, or has a boundary that vanishes (a loop): no vertex's coboundary is reduced then, and a bar's cocycle is the indicator of the component that dies. A complex with any other edge (a Morse complex can have one) reduces degree 0 like every other degree. The pairs and representatives are the same either way.

Value parameters

packSimplices

reduce simplices with Int vertices on flat arrays (see above). false reduces the cells themselves, with the same results, more slowly; reducesPacked tells which a stream gets.

useUnionFind

pair degree 0 by union-find where the complex allows (see above). false reduces the vertices' coboundaries, with the same results (for benchmarking and for checking the two against each other).

open class CellularHomologyEngine[CellT, CoefficientT, FiltrationT]

The naive persistence engine: the standard reduction algorithm, one cell at a time in filtration order. Each cell's boundary is reduced against the pivots recorded so far; a cell whose boundary reduces to zero opens a class, any other closes the class of its pivot. No clearing or other shortcuts: the reference the other engines are checked against.

The naive persistence engine: the standard reduction algorithm, one cell at a time in filtration order. Each cell's boundary is reduced against the pivots recorded so far; a cell whose boundary reduces to zero opens a class, any other closes the class of its pivot. No clearing or other shortcuts: the reference the other engines are checked against.

persistentHomology(stream) returns a cursor (HomologyState) that processes cells on demand: advanceTo(f), advanceFor(budget), advanceAll(), then diagramAt(f)/barcodeAt(f) for the diagram truncated at any f, with a representative cycle for every bar. The stream decides the top degree: cells of dimension k + 1 are needed for degree k, and the degree-(k + 1) bars of such a stream are incomplete.

Implementation note: chain arithmetic must order cells by the stream's filtration, so the RingModule instance is summoned inside HomologyState, where that ordering exists (a given fixes its own context when it is constructed).

abstract class Chain[CellT, CoefficientT]

A formal sum of cells with coefficients in a field, kept in an order on the cells: its leading term, the pivot of a reduction, is the least cell. Made by Chain(...), Chain.from and arithmetic.

A formal sum of cells with coefficients in a field, kept in an order on the cells: its leading term, the pivot of a reduction, is the least cell. Made by Chain(...), Chain.from and arithmetic.

The storage is open to experiment: a subclass passes the order and the field to this constructor and implements entryIterator, its stored entries. Every other member has a default built on those two, which a storage may override for speed; reductions (Chain.reduceBy), arithmetic, boundary, equality and the engines use these members only. The library keeps chains in a heap (what Chain(...) and arithmetic make), and the grid engines keep their representatives packed in arrays.

open class CholeskyWorkspace(capacity: Int)

Maintains a Cholesky factor of B_W for the current working set W.

Maintains a Cholesky factor of B_W for the current working set W.

The working set is kept linearly independent, so B_W stays positive definite and a plain Cholesky suffices; DAQP uses LDL^T so that it can represent the singular step, we instead detect it via the Schur complement and restructure the working set immediately (see DualQP).

Appending is the standard bordered update; deleting removes a row of L and rotates the resulting extra superdiagonal away with Givens rotations, which is O(|W|²) rather than a refactorisation.

object CircularCoordinates

Circular coordinates (de Silva, Morozov, Vejdemo-Johansson, "Persistent Cohomology and Circular Coordinates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 45:737-759, 2011): a map from the points to the circle R/Z that represents a persistent H¹ class of the Vietoris-Rips complex.

Circular coordinates (de Silva, Morozov, Vejdemo-Johansson, "Persistent Cohomology and Circular Coordinates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 45:737-759, 2011): a map from the points to the circle R/Z that represents a persistent H¹ class of the Vietoris-Rips complex.

Pick a scale r inside the class's bar (see h1Bars). The class is then an essential class of the fixed complex K_r, the complex truncated at r; it is matched to the bar of the full computation with the same birth, since truncation never changes a birth. Its cocycle, computed over F_prime and lifted to the integers, is smoothed to the harmonic representative: g minimizing ||z - d0 g||² over the connected component of K_r carrying the class, solved by conjugate gradients on the normal equations with one vertex fixed at 0. The coordinate of a point is g(v) mod 1. The solve follows DREiMac's toroidalcoords.py.

There are two ways in. compute(metricSpace, r, ...) takes the points and does everything itself, on the Vietoris-Rips complex. CircularCoordinates(diagram, input, ...) takes a PersistenceDiagram you already have, of any complex and from any engine, together with what it was computed from, and reads the bar, its field and (when the diagram carries cocycles) its cocycle from the diagram.

open class CubicalGridStream(val shape: IndexedSeq[Int], val topCellValue: IndexedSeq[Int] => Double, val parallelFiltrationValue: Boolean = ..., val nanMask: Boolean = ...) extends StratifiedCellStream[Cube, Double], DoubleFiltration[Cube]

The cubical complex of a full rectangular grid, filtered by the values of its top cells (pixels, voxels): every other cube gets the minimum value of the top cells containing it, the sublevel-set convention of GUDHI, DIPHA and Perseus. A face is contained in every top cell its cofaces are, so the filtration is monotone. For superlevel sets, negate the values (what CubicalImage's sublevel = false does).

The cubical complex of a full rectangular grid, filtered by the values of its top cells (pixels, voxels): every other cube gets the minimum value of the top cells containing it, the sublevel-set convention of GUDHI, DIPHA and Perseus. A face is contained in every top cell its cofaces are, so the filtration is monotone. For superlevel sets, negate the values (what CubicalImage's sublevel = false does).

A top cell of value Double.NaN is masked: it is not in the complex. NaN has no sign and compares to nothing, so it means the same in a sublevel and a superlevel image. Every other cube takes the minimum over the UNMASKED top cells containing it, and is not in the complex either when all of them are masked: the complex is the closure of the unmasked top cells. Infinite values are ordinary values: a top cell of value +Infinity enters at +Infinity. With nanMask = false masks are off: a NaN value is an error, naming the pixel, when the values are first read.

shape(i) is the number of pixels along axis i. The complex has prod_i (2 shape(i) + 1) cells (totalCellCount): a 256x256 image has 513² = 263169.

Cubical complexes of images and voxel grids. Every array constructor reduces to fromFlatArray: values in row-major order (last axis fastest) and a shape.

Infinite values are ordinary values: +Infinity enters after every finite value in a sublevel image, and before them in a superlevel one (negated to -Infinity). open class DelaunayPredicates(points: Array[Array[Double]])

Exact geometric predicates for Delaunay triangulation in dimensions 2 to 4: the sign of an orientation determinant and of an in-sphere determinant, each computed in floating point first and, when the result is too close to zero for the floating-point error bound, again in exact arithmetic (BigDecimal: a double is a binary fraction, so sums and products of doubles are exact there). In-sphere ties (a point exactly on a circumsphere) are broken by a symbolic perturbation of the lifted coordinate that depends only on the points' indices, so the result is the Delaunay triangulation of an infinitesimally perturbed point set: unique, whatever the insertion order.

In-sphere ties (a point exactly on a circumsphere) are broken by a symbolic perturbation of the lifted coordinate that depends only on the points' indices, so the result is the Delaunay triangulation of an infinitesimally perturbed point set: unique, whatever the insertion order.

Determinants are expanded over permutations, which is cheap up to 5x5 (in-sphere in 4-D) and grows as n! beyond.

open class DirectedFlagStream(val n: Int, edges: Iterable[(Int, Int, Double)], val maxDimension: Int, val maxFiltrationValue: Double = ..., vertexValue: Int => Double = ...) extends StratifiedCellStream[DirectedSimplex, Double], DoubleFiltration[DirectedSimplex]

The directed flag complex of a weighted directed graph (the construction of Flagser, Luetgehetmann, Govc, Smith and Levi 2020; Reimann et al. 2017 for the clique complex of a neural network): its cells are the ordered tuples of vertices (v0, ..., vk) such that every edge vi -> vj with i &lt; j is present, and a cell enters at the largest weight of those edges (or of its vertices, which enter at vertexValue, 0 by default).

The directed flag complex of a weighted directed graph (the construction of Flagser, Luetgehetmann, Govc, Smith and Levi 2020; Reimann et al. 2017 for the clique complex of a neural network): its cells are the ordered tuples of vertices (v0, ..., vk) such that every edge vi -> vj with i &lt; j is present, and a cell enters at the largest weight of those edges (or of its vertices, which enter at vertexValue, 0 by default).

A directed cycle a -> b -> c -> a is a hole: no tuple contains all three, so the three edges bound nothing. The same three vertices with a -> c in place of c -> a span the filled triangle (a, b, c). An undirected graph (both directions present) gives many more cells than its clique complex, one for every ordering of every clique.

val stream = DirectedFlagStream(4, Seq((0, 1, 1.0), (1, 2, 1.0), (2, 0, 1.0)), maxDimension = 1)
Persistence(stream).bettiNumbers   // Vector(1, 1): a loop

The complex is built for homological degrees 0 .. maxDimension (it holds the cells up to dimension maxDimension + 1), and every cell is held in memory.

Value parameters

edges

(from, to, weight), each ordered pair once; a pair and its reverse may both be present

maxFiltrationValue

cells entering later than this are left out

object DiscreteMorse

Discrete Morse theory on a filtered complex: apply finds a matching that respects the filtration (a pair enters at one value) and returns the MorseComplex.

Discrete Morse theory on a filtered complex: apply finds a matching that respects the filtration (a pair enters at one value) and returns the MorseComplex.

val rips = VietorisRips(points, maxDimension = 2)
val morse = DiscreteMorse(rips)
morse.critical.size                      // far fewer cells than `rips`
Persistence(morse.stream, maxDimension = 2)   // the same bars as Persistence(rips, maxDimension = 2)

The matching is made level by level, a level being the cells that enter at one value, by elementary collapses (Strategy.Reduction: a cell with exactly one coface in the level, paired with it) or by elementary coreductions (Strategy.Coreduction: a cell with exactly one face in the level, paired with it), and when neither applies the cell of highest (respectively lowest) dimension is left critical. Pairs inside one level are acyclic, and a gradient path never goes back up in the filtration, so the matching is acyclic as a whole; the pairs are the apparent pairs of Ripser and more.

object DistanceToMeasure

The empirical distance to measure (Chazal, Cohen-Steiner, Mérigot, "Geometric inference for probability measures", Found. Comput. Math. 11, 2011) with k neighbours:

The empirical distance to measure (Chazal, Cohen-Steiner, Mérigot, "Geometric inference for probability measures", Found. Comput. Math. 11, 2011) with k neighbours:

f(x) = ( (1/k) sum over the k nearest neighbours y of x of d(x, y)^q )^(1/q)

As in GUDHI, x counts among its own neighbours (so k = 1 gives f = 0) and q defaults to 2.

The SpatialQuery chooses the nearest-neighbour search. BruteForce works for any distances; VantagePointQuery requires the triangle inequality, which an ExplicitMetricSpace does not check.

open class DowkerGeometry(val relation: Array[Array[Double]])

The filtered Dowker complex of a relation R: L x W -> [0, Infinity] between two finite sets (C. H. Dowker, "Homology groups of relations", Ann. of Math. 56 (1952); filtered as in Chowdhury and Mémoli, "A functorial Dowker theorem and persistent homology of asymmetric networks", 2018). A set sigma of rows is a simplex at t when one witness w sees all of it by then:

The filtered Dowker complex of a relation R: L x W -> [0, Infinity] between two finite sets (C. H. Dowker, "Homology groups of relations", Ann. of Math. 56 (1952); filtered as in Chowdhury and Mémoli, "A functorial Dowker theorem and persistent homology of asymmetric networks", 2018). A set sigma of rows is a simplex at t when one witness w sees all of it by then:

f(sigma) = min_w max_{x in sigma} R(x, w)

R need not come from a metric. The unfiltered Dowker complex is the case R(x, w) in {0, Infinity} (DowkerGeometry.fromBoolean); the witness complex with nu = 0 is the case R = landmark-to-witness distances.

The filtration is monotone (f(tau) &lt;= f(sigma) for tau a face of sigma, since the max over a subset is smaller for every w), vertices have values min_w R(x, w) that are generally nonzero, and the complex is not a flag complex, so the Ripser engines do not apply (MATLAB and the CLI also do not offer chunks for relations).

'''Duality''': the complexes of R (on the rows) and of its transpose (dual, on the columns) are homotopy equivalent at every t, and their persistence modules are isomorphic, so their barcodes agree. This holds for the barcodes without zero-length bars, the default: with includeZeroLength = true the two sides differ, since each vertex contributes an H₀ birth and the sides have different numbers of vertices.

The DTM-filtration of Anai, Chazal, Glisse, Ike, Lecci, Rouvreau, Saulnier and Wasserman, "DTM-based filtrations" (arXiv:1811.04757, Prop. 3.5), a weighted Rips filtration with weights f(x) the distance to measure (DistanceToMeasure). Values are diameters, as in Vietoris-Rips and GUDHI; with f = 0 (as for k = 1) this is the Vietoris-Rips filtration. For p = 1 it agrees with GUDHI's DTMRipsComplex.

The DTM-filtration of Anai, Chazal, Glisse, Ike, Lecci, Rouvreau, Saulnier and Wasserman, "DTM-based filtrations" (arXiv:1811.04757, Prop. 3.5), a weighted Rips filtration with weights f(x) the distance to measure (DistanceToMeasure). Values are diameters, as in Vietoris-Rips and GUDHI; with f = 0 (as for k = 1) this is the Vietoris-Rips filtration. For p = 1 it agrees with GUDHI's DTMRipsComplex.

p is the ball-radius exponent of Def. 3.1 (not the exponent q of the distance to measure), 1 or 2:

  • p = 1: t(f_x, f_y, d) = max(f_x, f_y, (d + f_x + f_y) / 2), as in GUDHI;
  • p = 2: t = max(f_x, f_y, sqrt(u² + f_x²)) with u = (d² + f_y² - f_x²) / (2d) when |f_y² - f_x²| &lt;= d², and max(f_x, f_y) otherwise (one ball contains the other).

A flag complex on the weighted distances 2 t, with vertex x born at 2 f(x). maxFiltrationValue defaults to the minimum enclosing radius of the weighted distances, which is at least every vertex's birth and beyond which the complex is a cone. Vertices are born at nonzero values, so the Ripser engines do not apply.

open class DualQP(val n: Int, workingSetCapacity: Int, settings: AlphaDQPSettings)

Solves

Solves

maximise d(lambda) = -1/2 lambda^t B lambda + U^t lambda subject to lambda_i >= 0 for i not in J

which is the Lagrangian dual of Eq. (9) with H = I. Optimum equals the primal optimum c* = 1/2 ||y* - x||^2; the primal solution is recovered from the KKT conditions (12) as y* = x - sum_i lambda_i (x_i - x).

Reused across every candidate simplex sharing the same base vertex x -- only J changes, which is exactly the observation in the paper that lets B and U be assembled once per vertex rather than once per simplex.

The instance is stateful and not thread safe; give each worker its own.

object EdgeCollapse

Edge collapse of a Vietoris-Rips filtration (Boissonnat and Pritam, "Edge Collapse and Persistence of Flag Complexes", SoCG 2020; Glisse and Pritam, "Swap, Shift and Trim to Edge Collapse a Filtration", SoCG 2022): a smaller weighted graph whose flag complex has the same persistent homology at every scale, computed from the graph alone.

Edge collapse of a Vietoris-Rips filtration (Boissonnat and Pritam, "Edge Collapse and Persistence of Flag Complexes", SoCG 2020; Glisse and Pritam, "Swap, Shift and Trim to Edge Collapse a Filtration", SoCG 2022): a smaller weighted graph whose flag complex has the same persistent homology at every scale, computed from the graph alone.

An edge {u, v} is dominated by a vertex w when every common neighbour of u and v is a neighbour of w; removing a dominated edge (and the simplices containing it) from a flag complex is a collapse. Over a filtration, an edge's entry is postponed to the last scale at which it is still dominated, or the edge is removed if it stays dominated to the end. This is a port of GUDHI's single pass (Flag_complex_edge_collapser.h): edges in decreasing order of their original value, each decided once against the graph as it stands. The order matters: deciding the edges independently and iterating to a fixed point removes too much. One pass is not necessarily minimal, and collapsing the output again may shrink it further.

At every scale the collapsed complex is a subcomplex of the original, so a representative computed on it is a representative of the same class in the original complex.

Vietoris-Rips (or, with filtrationValueOverride, any filtration on the same vertex set that is monotone along faces), each dimension enumerated in full by SimplexIndexing's combinatorial number system and filtered by keepCriterion and maxFiltrationValue. What VietorisRips chooses between, with RipserCofaceSimplexStream.

Enumerating every vertex set of a dimension holds only while there are at most Int.MaxValue of them (a Range of indices); RipserCofaceSimplexStream, the default, builds each dimension from the cofaces of the cells it kept and has no such limit. object Erf

The error function erf(x) = 2/sqrt(pi) * integral_0^x exp(-t^2) dt and its complement erfc(x) = 1 - erf(x).

The error function erf(x) = 2/sqrt(pi) * integral_0^x exp(-t^2) dt and its complement erfc(x) = 1 - erf(x).

Computed by W. J. Cody's rational Chebyshev approximations ("Rational Chebyshev approximations for the error function", Mathematics of Computation 23, 1969): one in x on |x| &lt;= 0.46875, one in exp(-x^2) times a rational function of x up to 4, and one in 1/x^2 beyond. erf is accurate to 4e-16 absolute (a few units in the last place), erfc to a relative 2e-15 out to where it underflows (near x = 26.5). erf is exactly odd and exactly +-1 from |x| = 6.

open class EuclideanMetricSpace(val pts: Array[Array[Double]], val cacheDistances: Boolean = ...) extends FiniteMetricSpace[Int]

The Euclidean distances between the rows of pts (all of the same length).

The Euclidean distances between the rows of pts (all of the same length).

Value parameters

cacheDistances

compute all pairwise distances on first use and look them up afterwards (default true). That is n^2 doubles, about 8 MB at 1,000 points and 512 MB at 8,192, so the cache is only kept up to EuclideanMetricSpace.MaxCachedPoints points; above that every distance is computed when asked for. Pass false to compute every distance on demand at any size. Distances are looked up many times per pair during a Vietoris-Rips computation, so the cache usually pays off where it fits.

final case class EulerCharacteristicCurve(scales: IndexedSeq[Double], values: IndexedSeq[Long])

The Euler characteristic of a filtered complex as a function of the scale: the number of vertices, minus the edges, plus the triangles, ... of the cells with filtration value at most t. It is a step function, so the curve keeps the scales where it steps and the value from there on.

The Euler characteristic of a filtered complex as a function of the scale: the number of vertices, minus the edges, plus the triangles, ... of the cells with filtration value at most t. It is a step function, so the curve keeps the scales where it steps and the value from there on.

val curve = EulerCharacteristicCurve(points)               // Vietoris-Rips, simplices up to dimension 2
curve(0.3)                                                 // the Euler characteristic at scale 0.3
curve.sample(0.0, 1.0, 50)                                 // 50 evenly spaced samples

A vectorization that needs no persistence: EulerCharacteristicCurve.apply counts the cliques of every edge's lens graph, so it stores no simplices and sorts nothing.

Value parameters

scales

The scales where the curve changes, strictly increasing; for a point cloud the first is 0.0, where the vertices appear.

values

values(i) is the Euler characteristic from scales(i) up to (not including) scales(i + 1).

open class ExplicitMetricSpace(val dist: Seq[Seq[Double]]) extends FiniteMetricSpace[Int]

Takes in an explicit distance matrix, and performs lookups in this distance matrix.

Takes in an explicit distance matrix, and performs lookups in this distance matrix.

Value parameters

dist

Distance matrix represented as a Seq[Seq[Double]]. The class expects but does not enforce:

  • dist(x1).size == dist(x2).size for all x1,x2
  • dist(x).size == dist.size for all x
  • dist(x)(x) == 0 for all x
  • dist(x)(y) == dist(y)(x) for all x,y
  • The triangle inequality Only the lower triangle is read: distance(x, y) is dist(max(x, y))(min(x, y)), as in Ripser and GUDHI, so a matrix that is not exactly symmetric gives the same results here as there.

open class FastAlphaHomologyEngine[CoefficientT]

Persistent homology of a Helix alpha complex by union-find instead of matrix reduction: degree 0 on the vertices and edges, the top degree d - 1 on the dual graph of the top-dimensional simplices, as in FastCubicalHomologyEngine. In the plane those cover everything; in dimension 3 and up the degrees in between are computed by the cohomology engine on the complex without its top simplices. Works in any ambient dimension from 2, with representatives for every bar.

Persistent homology of a Helix alpha complex by union-find instead of matrix reduction: degree 0 on the vertices and edges, the top degree d - 1 on the dual graph of the top-dimensional simplices, as in FastCubicalHomologyEngine. In the plane those cover everything; in dimension 3 and up the degrees in between are computed by the cohomology engine on the complex without its top simplices. Works in any ambient dimension from 2, with representatives for every bar.

The dual graph needs every facet to have one or two top-dimensional cofaces. Unlike a grid, a triangulation does not guarantee it, so it is checked first, throwing FastAlphaTriangulationException when it fails (rare on random points). A facet's dual-edge value is its own filtration value, which can be smaller than its cofaces' circumradii (a Gabriel edge).

open class FastCubicalHomologyEngine[CoefficientT]

Persistent homology of a cubical grid by union-find instead of matrix reduction (after Le Breton, Szustakowski and Piraud, arXiv:2606.04801, extended here to any coefficient field and to representatives): degree 0 by union-find on the vertices and edges, the top degree d - 1 (d the grid's dimension) by union-find on the dual graph. In 2-D those cover everything; in dimension 3 and up the degrees in between are computed by the cohomology engine on the grid without its top cells. Requires d >= 2. A NaN (masked) pixel is not in the complex (see CubicalGridStream).

Persistent homology of a cubical grid by union-find instead of matrix reduction (after Le Breton, Szustakowski and Piraud, arXiv:2606.04801, extended here to any coefficient field and to representatives): degree 0 by union-find on the vertices and edges, the top degree d - 1 (d the grid's dimension) by union-find on the dual graph. In 2-D those cover everything; in dimension 3 and up the degrees in between are computed by the cohomology engine on the grid without its top cells. Requires d >= 2. A NaN (masked) pixel is not in the complex (see CubicalGridStream).

The dual graph: the top cells (pixels) are vertices, the codimension-1 cells (facets) edges between the one or two top cells containing them, with one extra vertex ∞, at value +Infinity, on the far side of every facet on the boundary of the grid. By Alexander duality, degree d - 1 of the sublevel filtration is degree 0 of the dual graph's superlevel filtration: union-find in decreasing value with the elder rule, each merge giving the primal bar with birth and death swapped. ∞'s component never dies. A masked pixel is in the complement from the start, as ∞ is, and so is a facet between two masked pixels or a masked pixel and the outside: a component holding one is elder to every other but ∞'s, and when it dies at a facet of value v the primal class is born at v and never dies.

Representatives: each top cell carries a sign in its dual component, kept consistent as components merge (the sign flip is solved from the merging facet's two boundary coefficients, both ±1) so that interior facets cancel; when a component dies, its representative is the boundary of its signed sum of top cells. A merge costs nearly constant time; a representative costs time proportional to its region, and only reported bars get one.

open class FlagComplex(val graph: WeightedGraph, val maxDimension: Int, maxFiltrationValue: Optional[Double] = ...) extends StratifiedCellStream[Simplex[Int], Double], DoubleFiltration[Simplex[Int]]

The flag (clique) complex of a weighted graph: a set of vertices is a simplex when every two of them are joined by an edge, and it enters at the largest weight among those edges, so the filtration by weight is the Vietoris-Rips filtration of the graph read as a distance matrix with Infinity where there is no edge. Unlike VietorisRips(graph), it never forms the n x n matrix or its bit tables: cliques are grown from the sorted neighbour lists, so the cost is the number of simplices and the size of the graph, which is what makes a sparse network with a hundred thousand vertices feasible.

The flag (clique) complex of a weighted graph: a set of vertices is a simplex when every two of them are joined by an edge, and it enters at the largest weight among those edges, so the filtration by weight is the Vietoris-Rips filtration of the graph read as a distance matrix with Infinity where there is no edge. Unlike VietorisRips(graph), it never forms the n x n matrix or its bit tables: cliques are grown from the sorted neighbour lists, so the cost is the number of simplices and the size of the graph, which is what makes a sparse network with a hundred thousand vertices feasible.

val graph = WeightedGraph.unweighted(5, Seq((0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 0)))
Persistence(graph).bettiNumbers   // Vector(1, 1): the pentagon is a loop

The stream holds the simplices up to dimension maxDimension + 1, all in memory: cliques of a dense graph are many.

Value parameters

maxFiltrationValue

simplices entering later than this are left out; by default the graph's longest edge, past which nothing enters

A stream of simplices with Int vertices and Double values that can hand over its dimensions as flat arrays, without building a Simplex for each cell. A cohomology engine (CellularCohomologyEngine) reduces such a stream straight from the arrays, and builds a Simplex only for the cells of the representatives it returns.

A stream of simplices with Int vertices and Double values that can hand over its dimensions as flat arrays, without building a Simplex for each cell. A cohomology engine (CellularCohomologyEngine) reduces such a stream straight from the arrays, and builds a Simplex only for the cells of the representatives it returns.

The coface streams behind Cech, Witness, Dowker, DtmRips and SparseRips are the implementations. To build a new filtered complex on arrays, extend RipserCofaceSimplexStream and give it a RipserCofaceSimplexStream.FlatFiltration.

class GridRanks

The pixel (top cell) values of a cubical grid with their dense ranks: distinct holds the distinct values in ascending java.lang.Double.compare order, and rank(p) is the position of pixel p's value in it. In the T-construction every cell takes the smallest value of the pixels containing it, so every cell's value is some pixel's and its rank is the smallest rank among those pixels: the grid engines order cells by integer ranks and look the values up only to report them or compare them.

The pixel (top cell) values of a cubical grid with their dense ranks: distinct holds the distinct values in ascending java.lang.Double.compare order, and rank(p) is the position of pixel p's value in it. In the T-construction every cell takes the smallest value of the pixels containing it, so every cell's value is some pixel's and its rank is the smallest rank among those pixels: the grid engines order cells by integer ranks and look the values up only to report them or compare them.

Pixels are row-major, the last axis fastest. A NaN pixel is masked (not in the complex, see CubicalGridStream): it has no place in distinct and its rank is masked, one past every real rank. A minimum over ranks therefore skips masked pixels, and a cell's rank is masked exactly when every pixel containing it is masked.

open class HelixDelaunay(pts: Array[Array[Double]], seed: Long = ..., requireValidTriangulation: Boolean = ...)(using factor: EpsilonFactor) extends DelaunayAlphaShapes

The Delaunay triangulation of a point cloud, built by an incremental frontier walk (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?tp=&arnumber=10917453), filtered as an alpha complex.

The Delaunay triangulation of a point cloud, built by an incremental frontier walk (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?tp=&arnumber=10917453), filtered as an alpha complex.

The walk starts from a hull facet found by gift wrapping and, across each frontier facet, takes the point whose sphere through the facet is met first: one pass over the points per facet. Points that are exactly cospherical (grids) are tiled as a cluster. Every result is checked cheaply (each point a vertex, no facet in three top simplices, every boundary facet on the convex hull); a result that fails is re-triangulated from slightly perturbed points, with every radius recomputed from the original coordinates. The perturbation (1e-4 of the point spacing) decides how exact ties are broken, and can also flip a near-tie closer than that. The same pts and seed always give the same triangulation.

Limitation: a very small Epsilon (far below the default 1e-5) can leave an exactly degenerate input (a 3-D grid) with an invalid triangulation when the perturbed retriangulation does not converge.

Value parameters

pts

the points to triangulate

requireValidTriangulation

off by default. When on, the triangulation is also checked for cavities (a homology computation), and a result that cannot be repaired raises an exception instead of being returned as it is.

seed

seeds the perturbation used when a triangulation has to be repaired; general-position input does not depend on it.

final case class Image(values: IndexedSeq[Double], shape: IndexedSeq[Int], sublevel: Boolean = ..., nanMask: Boolean = ...)

A grayscale image (or voxel grid) for Persistence(Image(...)): values in row-major order, shape its size per axis. Sublevel filtration by default (dark regions first); sublevel = false for superlevel. A pixel of value Double.NaN is masked (missing data): it is not in the complex, in either direction (NaN has no sign). Infinite values are ordinary values: Double.PositiveInfinity enters after every finite value of a sublevel image and before them in a superlevel one, Double.NegativeInfinity the reverse. nanMask = false turns masks off, for data where a NaN can only be a bug: a NaN pixel is then an error, naming the pixel.

open class IncrementalVietorisRipsSimplexStream(metricSpace: FiniteMetricSpace[Int], val maxDimension: Int, maxFiltrationValue: Option[Double] = ..., keepCriterion: PartialFunction[Simplex[Int], Boolean] = ..., useLargestNeighborBound: Boolean = ...) extends EnumeratingCofaceSimplexStream

A reference Vietoris-Rips construction following Rieser's New-VR algorithm ("A New Construction of the Vietoris-Rips Complex", arXiv:2301.07191v3, Algorithms 1-4), kept close to the paper as a baseline for the faster constructions. Built eagerly, layer by layer (layer k + 1 from layer k and its candidate lists), the breadth-first reading of the paper's recursion, so any dimension can be served in any order.

A reference Vietoris-Rips construction following Rieser's New-VR algorithm ("A New Construction of the Vietoris-Rips Complex", arXiv:2301.07191v3, Algorithms 1-4), kept close to the paper as a baseline for the faster constructions. Built eagerly, layer by layer (layer k + 1 from layer k and its candidate lists), the breadth-first reading of the paper's recursion, so any dimension can be served in any order.

maxFiltrationValue (default Infinity) defines the graph whose clique complex is built: {i, j} is an edge iff distance(i, j) &lt;= maxFiltrationValue. The largestNeighbor table (L in Algorithm 2) only shortens scans. Every simplex is reached exactly once, so nothing needs deduplicating. Unlike Algorithm 4, which always includes the edges, maxDimension is the top simplex dimension served, so maxDimension = 0 gives the vertices only.

object Involution

Cycle representatives from a persistence pairing, by involuted persistent homology (Čufar and Virk, "Fast computation of persistent homology representatives with involuted persistent homology", arXiv:2105.03629).

Cycle representatives from a persistence pairing, by involuted persistent homology (Čufar and Virk, "Fast computation of persistent homology representatives with involuted persistent homology", arXiv:2105.03629).

Given the pairing a cohomology engine found, only the boundary columns of death cells are reduced: a column that reduces to zero never supplies a pivot, so leaving those out changes no reduced column. For a finite bar (σ, τ) the cycle is R_τ, the reduced boundary of τ: its youngest cell is σ, and it is the boundary of a chain whose youngest cell is τ. For an essential bar it is the cycle σ - Σ c V_τ' that the reduction of ∂σ to zero produces.

The pairing must come from the same total order as youngestFirst; every pivot is checked against the paired birth cell, and a mismatch throws.

abstract class Lab(characteristic: Int, precision: Double = ...)

What every lab shares: a coefficient field chosen by its characteristic (0 for Double compared within precision, a prime p for Z/p), with CoefficientT, Fp(...) and the field's given; flat re-exports of the whole library and the sset add-on, so import lab.{*, given} is the only import a lab user needs; and cats' .show syntax. Concrete labs add the conveniences of their setting: TDAlab (simplicial), CubicalLab. Engines never consult a lab: it is for writing chain algebra by hand.

object LatticeReduction

Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász lattice basis reduction of a Gram matrix (Scoccola, Gakhar, Bush, Schonsheck, Rask, Zhou, Perea, "Toroidal Coordinates: Decorrelating Circular Coordinates With Lattice Reduction", arXiv:2212.07201, Algorithm 4). Given the Gram matrix G of k independent vectors, factor G = C Cᵀ (Cholesky), run LLL on the rows of C, and return the unimodular integer change of basis: the shortest, most nearly orthogonal basis of the same lattice. CircularCoordinates.computeToroidal uses it to choose among the equally valid bases of a group of H¹ classes.

Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász lattice basis reduction of a Gram matrix (Scoccola, Gakhar, Bush, Schonsheck, Rask, Zhou, Perea, "Toroidal Coordinates: Decorrelating Circular Coordinates With Lattice Reduction", arXiv:2212.07201, Algorithm 4). Given the Gram matrix G of k independent vectors, factor G = C Cᵀ (Cholesky), run LLL on the rows of C, and return the unimodular integer change of basis: the shortest, most nearly orthogonal basis of the same lattice. CircularCoordinates.computeToroidal uses it to choose among the equally valid bases of a group of H¹ classes.

The Gram-Schmidt step projects onto the orthogonalized vectors, as in the textbook algorithm. DREiMac's _gram_schmidt projects onto the original ones, which agrees for k = 2 but not for k >= 3, so results can differ from DREiMac's there.

open class LayeredInorderSimplexStream(metricSpace: FiniteMetricSpace[Int], maxFiltrationValue: Option[Double] = ..., val candidates: Candidates = ...) extends EnumeratingCofaceSimplexStream

Vietoris-Rips, each dimension generated from the one below already in filtration order, so nothing above the edges is sorted (Bauer, Matuszewski and Vejdemo-Johansson, "Generating cofaces in Vietoris-Rips filtration order", arXiv:2411.05495, Theorem 3 and Proposition 7).

Vietoris-Rips, each dimension generated from the one below already in filtration order, so nothing above the edges is sorted (Bauer, Matuszewski and Vejdemo-Johansson, "Generating cofaces in Vietoris-Rips filtration order", arXiv:2411.05495, Theorem 3 and Proposition 7).

A simplex of diameter α is generated by exactly one of its facets, which has the same diameter, so walking dimension d in filtration order and emitting each simplex's same-diameter cofacets walks dimension d + 1 in filtration order. Each simplex carries its first longest edge, which its cofacets inherit unchanged and which decides the vertices it may add. Ties are listed colexicographically descending, as EnumeratingCofaceSimplexStream lists them: same cells, values and order. maxFiltrationValue defaults to the minimum enclosing radius.

Every dimension built so far is kept, as primitive arrays (LayeredInorderSimplexStream.Layer).

object MapAlgebra

Image, kernel and cokernel of a map of persistence modules that are sums of interval modules, over any field.

Image, kernel and cokernel of a map of persistence modules that are sums of interval modules, over any field.

The source has bars [b_i, d_i) and the target [b'_j, d'_j); the map is a matrix with a coefficient for each pair of a source bar i and a target bar j, given column by column (columns(i) maps j to the coefficient). A coefficient can be nonzero only where there is a map of interval modules at all, b'_j &lt;= b_i &lt; d'_j &lt;= d_i (isLegal): the generator of bar i, born at b_i, goes to the component of the target alive then, and the source dies no sooner than the component does.

Each result is a list of bars as (bar index, interval); the interval is [birth, death) in the numbers of the input. The three are computed by one kind of reduction, with the elder rule:

  • the image is the submodule of the target generated by the images of the source generators, each born at its bar's birth; reducing the generators in order of birth, with the target components ordered by death, a generator that does not reduce to zero is a bar from its birth to the death of its leading component;
  • the cokernel is the target modulo the image; its generators are the target bars, and the relations are the images of the source generators at their births and each target bar's own death. Taking relations in order of time, with the generators ordered by birth, a relation that does not reduce to zero kills the youngest generator in it at its time;
  • the kernel is the cokernel of the dual map, in the reversed order of the filtration (a bar [b, d) becomes [-d, -b)).

The tests check all three against the ranks of the structure maps of the modules, computed by linear algebra.

final class MorseComplex[CellT]

A discrete Morse complex of a filtered complex: an acyclic matching of cells into pairs (a, b) with a a face of b of one dimension less and both entering at the same filtration value, the cells left over (the critical cells) and the Morse boundary between them. Its persistent homology is that of the filtered complex it comes from, and it has fewer cells, often far fewer: Persistence(morse.stream) computes the barcode on the critical cells, and morse.lift takes a representative back to the original complex. Build it with DiscreteMorse.

A discrete Morse complex of a filtered complex: an acyclic matching of cells into pairs (a, b) with a a face of b of one dimension less and both entering at the same filtration value, the cells left over (the critical cells) and the Morse boundary between them. Its persistent homology is that of the filtered complex it comes from, and it has fewer cells, often far fewer: Persistence(morse.stream) computes the barcode on the critical cells, and morse.lift takes a representative back to the original complex. Build it with DiscreteMorse.

The Morse boundary of a critical cell τ is found by flowing its boundary down the gradient: a face a that is the lower member of a pair (a, b) is replaced by the other faces of b (subtracting ∂b times the coefficient of a over the incidence of a in b), until only critical cells, and cells matched with a face below them, remain, and the latter are dropped. It is computed in the coefficients asked for, so a pair needs an incidence of +1 or -1, which is a unit in every field.

final class PackedChain[CellT, CoefficientT](val keys: Array[Int], val coefficients: Array[AnyRef], val decoder: CellDecoder[CellT])(order: Ordering[CellT], field: is[CoefficientT, Field]) extends Chain[CellT, CoefficientT]

A chain stored packed, as the grid engines store representatives: keys(i) is a cell's key, which decoder turns into the cell, and coefficients(i) its coefficient. The keys are distinct and their cells ascending under the chain's order; every coefficient is nonzero. Nothing else is stored: reading the chain decodes its cells afresh (nothing is cached, so reading it does not make it bigger), and arithmetic on it gives a heap chain. The decoder and the order are kept by every chain they serve, so they must hold only what they need, never an engine.

open class PackedCubicalCohomologyEngine[C](grid: CubicalGridStream, topDim: Int, ranks: GridRanks, useApparentPairs: Boolean = ..., useUnionFind: Boolean = ...)(using evidence$1: Field { type Self = C; })

Persistent cohomology of a cubical grid by Bauer's Ripser algorithm on the grid itself: what CellularCohomologyEngine computes on a CubicalGridStream, or on its cells up to dimension topDim as a LimitedCubicalGridStream shows them -- the same bars, pairs, cocycles and cycles, term for term and in the same list order -- without a Cube, a hash of one or a Chain inside the reduction.

Persistent cohomology of a cubical grid by Bauer's Ripser algorithm on the grid itself: what CellularCohomologyEngine computes on a CubicalGridStream, or on its cells up to dimension topDim as a LimitedCubicalGridStream shows them -- the same bars, pairs, cocycles and cycles, term for term and in the same list order -- without a Cube, a hash of one or a Chain inside the reduction.

A cell is its index in the doubled grid (KMM encoding, see Cube). Within a dimension cells are ordered by the rank of their value (GridRanks) and then by index: the generic engine's order there, value ascending, then the encoding ascending. Boundaries and coboundaries come from index arithmetic. Clearing as in the generic engine; apparent pairs (a cell whose oldest same-value cofacet has it as its youngest same-value facet) are paired without a reduction and their columns rebuilt when another column needs them, which changes no output (useApparentPairs = false turns them off). Degree 0 is paired by union-find over the edges, the elder rule, with the indicator of the dying component as the cocycle (useUnionFind = false reduces the vertices' coboundaries instead, with the same output). Cycles come from the involution on the same pairs, specialised to packed cells as PackedRipserCohomologyEngine does it. A cell every pixel around which is masked (NaN) is not in the complex: it has rank GridRanks.masked, and is never listed nor met as a cofacet.

open class PackedRipserCohomologyEngine[CoefficientT](metricSpace: FiniteMetricSpace[Int], maxDimension: Int, useApparentPairs: Boolean = ..., maxFiltrationValue: Option[Double] = ..., neighbourLists: Option[Boolean] = ..., wideIndices: Option[Boolean] = ..., useEmergentPairs: Boolean = ..., useUnionFind: Boolean = ...)(using evidence$1: Field { type Self = CoefficientT; })

Persistent cohomology of the Vietoris-Rips complex of a metric space by Bauer's Ripser algorithm (arXiv:1908.02518): the fast engine for Vietoris-Rips, and the MATLAB/CLI default there. Cells are packed as (diameter, combinatorial index) pairs (DiameterIndex, Ripser's diameter_index_t); clearing, apparent pairs, emergent pairs and the enclosing-radius cutoff as in Ripser.

Persistent cohomology of the Vietoris-Rips complex of a metric space by Bauer's Ripser algorithm (arXiv:1908.02518): the fast engine for Vietoris-Rips, and the MATLAB/CLI default there. Cells are packed as (diameter, combinatorial index) pairs (DiameterIndex, Ripser's diameter_index_t); clearing, apparent pairs, emergent pairs and the enclosing-radius cutoff as in Ripser.

Reports degrees 0 .. maxDimension, each bar with its representative cocycle over DiameterIndex cells: decode a cell of a degree-k bar with vertices(cell, k + 1). maxFiltrationValue defaults to the minimum enclosing radius, past which nothing new is born. useApparentPairs = false, useEmergentPairs = false and useUnionFind = false turn off the apparent-pair shortcut, the emergent-pair shortcut and the pairing of degree 0 by union-find over the edges (the elder rule, as Ripser does it), which change no output (for benchmarking). An emergent pair is a column whose oldest cofacet of the same diameter is the pivot of no earlier column: it is paired with that cofacet without being reduced, and kept only as the simplex that makes it (rebuilt if a later column needs it), which saves the memory of its stored column.

Under a threshold that keeps few of the pairs (a large point cloud with a small maxFiltrationValue), cofacets are found from each vertex's list of neighbours within the threshold instead of by trying every vertex, as Ripser does with a sparse distance matrix. The lists are built when at most a quarter of all pairs are within the threshold (neighbourLists = Some(true) or Some(false) decides it instead); the output is the same either way.

The combinatorial index of a simplex is one Long while the indices of every simplex up to dimension maxDimension + 1 fit in one, and two words (WideSimplexIndexing, up to 126 bits) beyond: for 16,000 points to degree 3, or 122,000 to degree 2. The choice is made before the run (wideIndices decides it instead) and changes no output.

object ParallelPackedCohomology

The engine behind Persistence.Engine.ParallelRipser (#192, #194, #220): Vietoris-Rips persistent cohomology over F_p on implicit coboundaries, as the packed Ripser engine computes it (clearing, apparent pairs, a heap working column, cofacets enumerated on the fly), with each degree's columns cut into units of whole edge blocks and the units reduced in parallel. A column whose pivot leaves its unit is deferred: the deferred columns go on in parallel while their pivots are owned by the units' pairs (phase 2a), then one by one in the sequential order (phase 2b). The pairs, and the reduction log of every column, are those of one sequential reduction in the same order.

The engine behind Persistence.Engine.ParallelRipser (#192, #194, #220): Vietoris-Rips persistent cohomology over F_p on implicit coboundaries, as the packed Ripser engine computes it (clearing, apparent pairs, a heap working column, cofacets enumerated on the fly), with each degree's columns cut into units of whole edge blocks and the units reduced in parallel. A column whose pivot leaves its unit is deferred: the deferred columns go on in parallel while their pivots are owned by the units' pairs (phase 2a), then one by one in the sequential order (phase 2b). The pairs, and the reduction log of every column, are those of one sequential reduction in the same order.

A simplex is one Long key: its block (1 + the rank of its first longest edge, edges ranked by (length, smaller end, larger end); 0 for a vertex) above mask - index (index its combinatorial index; a larger index is older, as in the packed engine). Within one dimension, ascending keys are the filtration order, oldest first. When the block and the index do not fit in one Long together (Space.wide), a key is two words: mask - index, which still names the simplex within its dimension, and the block beside it in every array, heap and column that orders keys; the order is then by block, then key. Coefficients are Ints mod p.

persistence(space, threads, unitsPerThread, ...) cuts each degree into threads * unitsPerThread units; they run on the threads Parallel has where the call is (Parallel.withThreads(n), else the common pool), one after the other when threads is 1 and on JavaScript. threads 1 with 1 unit per thread is the sequential reduction. The command-line driver is ParallelPackedCohomologyDriver (JVM, in the test tree).

object PersistenceFilter

Dropping short bars, relative to the scale of the input: the policy behind diagram.longerThanFraction(), bars.longerThanFraction() and the MATLAB/CLI default. (Zero-length bars are already gone: engines leave them out unless asked. For a fixed threshold, longerThan(eps) is simpler.)

Dropping short bars, relative to the scale of the input: the policy behind diagram.longerThanFraction(), bars.longerThanFraction() and the MATLAB/CLI default. (Zero-length bars are already gone: engines leave them out unless asked. For a fixed threshold, longerThan(eps) is simpler.)

This is a rule of thumb for what to show, not a statistical test: it keeps a bar because it is long compared with the data's scale, not because it is unlikely to be noise. For a threshold that comes from the sample itself, see BootstrapBand.

'''The scale.''' A bar is judged against a scale the caller supplies: for a point cloud or distance matrix, metricSpace.minimumEnclosingRadius (Ripser's enclosing radius: past it the Vietoris-Rips complex is a cone and nothing new is born, so every bar lies in [0, scale]; it is also the default Vietoris-Rips truncation); for a cubical image, the range of its values. It is used in the units the complex reports (diameters for Vietoris-Rips, radii for Cech/alpha). Without such a quantity, filtrationRange, the span of the barcode's own finite endpoints, is the fallback.

'''The rule.''' A bar is kept iff it is essential or its persistence is strictly greater than the threshold. A threshold &lt;= 0 keeps everything.

class PersistenceMap[S, T, C]

The map on persistent homology that a map of filtered complexes induces, and its image, kernel and cokernel as barcodes: what survives from the smaller space in the larger, what dies on the way in, and what only the larger one sees.

The map on persistent homology that a map of filtered complexes induces, and its image, kernel and cokernel as barcodes: what survives from the smaller space in the larger, what dies on the way in, and what only the larger one sees.

val sub = Persistence(points.take(30), maxDimension = 2, includeZeroLength = true)
val whole = Persistence(points, maxDimension = 2, includeZeroLength = true)
val inclusion = PersistenceMap.inclusion(sub, whole)
inclusion.image(1)      // the loops of the subsample, as far as they stay loops in the whole
inclusion.cokernel(1)   // the loops that only the whole sample has

For each degree the matrix has a row for each bar of the target and a column for each bar of the source: column i is the pushforward of the source bar's representative cycle, written in the target's bars at the time the source bar is born. The bars are those of the diagrams without the zero-length ones (a class that never exists), and sourceBars and targetBars give them in the order the matrix uses.

The map must send each cell to a chain of cells that have already entered the target by the time the cell enters the source (it preserves the filtration). Both diagrams need representative cycles and the cells of their bars (the default of Persistence); the target must keep its zero-length bars, includeZeroLength = true, because their representatives are part of what the reduction reads. They must be over the same field: the same characteristic (or the same coefficients).

object PersistentLaplacian

The persistent Laplacian of a filtered complex (Wang, Nguyen and Wei; Mémoli, Wan and Wang): a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix Δ_k^{s,t} on the k-cells of the complex at s, for every pair s H_k(K_t), and whose other eigenvalues carry geometric information the barcode does not (the smallest nonzero one is a persistent spectral gap).

The persistent Laplacian of a filtered complex (Wang, Nguyen and Wei; Mémoli, Wan and Wang): a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix Δ_k^{s,t} on the k-cells of the complex at s, for every pair s H_k(K_t), and whose other eigenvalues carry geometric information the barcode does not (the smallest nonzero one is a persistent spectral gap).

val rips = VietorisRips(points, maxDimension = 1)
val laplacian = PersistentLaplacian(rips, dimension = 1, from = 0.4, to = 0.9)
laplacian.bettiNumber     // loops at 0.4 that are still loops at 0.9
laplacian.spectralGap     // the smallest nonzero eigenvalue
laplacian.eigenvalues     // ascending

With C^{s,t}_{k+1} the chains of K_t whose boundary lies in K_s, the persistent Laplacian is ∂ ∂^* + ∂_k^{s *} ∂_k^s, the first term being the boundary of C^{s,t}_{k+1} into the k-chains of K_s composed with its adjoint, in the inner product in which the cells are orthonormal. Written with the matrices of K_t and its rows split into those in K_s (D) and those in K_t \ K_s (R), that is D (1 - R^+ R) D^T + A^T A, A being the boundary of the k-cells of K_s; at s = t it is the Hodge Laplacian. The coefficients are real numbers, the matrices dense: for complexes of a few thousand cells in the dimension asked for. The stream has to hold the cells of dimension dimension + 1 (a stream cut off at homological degree k does, up to k).

object Phat

PHAT's boundary-matrix formats, with the conventions of phat/boundary_matrix.h (load_ascii, save_ascii, load_binary, save_binary): a matrix over Z/2 whose columns are numbered from 0, each with a dimension and the sorted row indices of its nonzero entries.

PHAT's boundary-matrix formats, with the conventions of phat/boundary_matrix.h (load_ascii, save_ascii, load_binary, save_binary): a matrix over Z/2 whose columns are numbered from 0, each with a dimension and the sorted row indices of its nonzero entries.

  • ASCII: one column per line, the dimension first and then the row indices, separated by whitespace; empty lines and lines starting with # are skipped.
  • Binary: an Int64 column count, then for each column its dimension (Int64), its number of entries N (Int64) and the N row indices (Int64). PHAT writes the machine's byte order; this reader and writer use little-endian, which is the byte order of x86 and ARM machines.

PHAT reads a matrix whose columns are in filtration order, so a face's row comes before the column of its coface: fromStream builds that matrix from a stream, sorting its cells by the stream's filtrationOrdering.

trait PowerDistance

The data the algorithm needs: a finite set of sites with power weights.

The data the algorithm needs: a finite set of sites with power weights.

Everything in the QP is expressible through squared distances alone, because

B_ij = (x_i - x)·(x_j - x) = ( d²(i,x) + d²(j,x) - d²(i,j) ) / 2 U_i = ( p(i) - p(x) - d²(i,x) ) / 2

so the solver never sees coordinates. Coordinates are optional and used only to materialise the witness map Phi (Definition 11).

Caveat: the QP is convex only if B is positive semidefinite, i.e. only if the squared distances come from a Euclidean embedding. Feeding in a non-Euclidean metric (as Vietoris-Rips happily allows) is not supported; the notion of "alpha complex" is not defined there either.

final case class ProductCell[A, B](left: A, right: B)(context: Context[A, B])

A cell left × right of the product of two cell complexes, of dimension dim(left) + dim(right), with the boundary ∂(a × b) = ∂a × b + (-1)^dim(a) a × ∂b (so ∂∂ = 0 over any field). Two product cells are equal when their factors are: the context is how the cell knows the structure of its factors, not part of its identity.

object ProductComplex

The product of two filtered complexes as a stream: a cell σ × τ for every pair of a cell of each, entering at the larger of the two values (Combine.Max, the default: the sublevel set at t is the product of the two sublevel sets) or at their sum (Combine.Sum: the tensor product of the two filtered chain complexes).

The product of two filtered complexes as a stream: a cell σ × τ for every pair of a cell of each, entering at the larger of the two values (Combine.Max, the default: the sublevel set at t is the product of the two sublevel sets) or at their sum (Combine.Sum: the tensor product of the two filtered chain complexes).

val circle = VietorisRips(points, maxDimension = 2)
val interval = VietorisRips(otherPoints, maxDimension = 2)
Persistence(ProductComplex(circle, interval))        // the homology of the product, by any engine
Barcode.kunneth(bars1, bars2)                         // the same bars from the bars of the factors

Both streams are held in memory, and the product has a cell for every pair, so this is for factors of a few hundred cells each. A factor cut off at a homological degree k (homologyDegreeLimit) makes the product accurate to the smaller of the two degrees. The bars carry chains of ProductCells, (left, right) being the cells of the factors.

object Relative

The pair (X, A) as a stream: the cells of X that are not in the subcomplex A, with boundaries that leave out the faces in A, so that its persistent homology is the relative one, H(X_t, A_t) with A_t = A ∩ X_t.

The pair (X, A) as a stream: the cells of X that are not in the subcomplex A, with boundaries that leave out the faces in A, so that its persistent homology is the relative one, H(X_t, A_t) with A_t = A ∩ X_t.

val rips = VietorisRips(points, maxDimension = 2)
Persistence(Relative.ofVertices(rips, Set(0, 1, 2)))   // the pairs of the Rips complex modulo the one on 0, 1, 2

The subcomplex has to be closed under faces (a face of a cell in A is in A), and each of its cells enters X no later than it would as a cell of X on its own; neither is checked. The bars carry chains of RelativeCells, the cell of X being cell. For a connected complex whose vertices all enter together, relative to one vertex, that is the reduced homology: the bar of the whole complex in degree 0 is gone and the rest stays.

maxFiltrationValue defaults to the minimum enclosing radius, past which the complex is a cone and nothing new is born, so the barcode is the same as untruncated. memoizeFiltrationValue caches every diameter it computes (faster, more memory); off by default.

open class SheehyRipsSimplexStream(val ambientMetricSpace: FiniteMetricSpace[Int], val permutation: GreedyPermutation, val epsilon: Double, keepCriterion: PartialFunction[Simplex[Int], Boolean] = ..., maxFiltrationValue: Option[Double] = ..., parallelFiltrationValue: Boolean = ...) extends RipserCofaceSimplexStream

The sparse Vietoris-Rips filtration of Cavanna, Jahanseir and Sheehy, "A Geometric Perspective on Sparse Filtrations" (arXiv:1506.03797, CCCG 2015): the greedy-permutation form of Sheehy's linear-size approximation ("Linear-Size Approximations to the Vietoris-Rips Filtration", DCG 2013, arXiv:1203.6786). Its barcode is a (1 + epsilon)-multiplicative approximation of the Vietoris-Rips barcode (Theorem 5), from a complex of size linear in the number of points for data of bounded doubling dimension. (Sheehy 2013's epsilon is a different parameter: its factor is 1/(1 - 2 epsilon).) The edges are computed from all pairs, O(n^2), rather than by the paper's O(n log n) neighbour search: the complex to reduce is small, its construction is not.

The sparse Vietoris-Rips filtration of Cavanna, Jahanseir and Sheehy, "A Geometric Perspective on Sparse Filtrations" (arXiv:1506.03797, CCCG 2015): the greedy-permutation form of Sheehy's linear-size approximation ("Linear-Size Approximations to the Vietoris-Rips Filtration", DCG 2013, arXiv:1203.6786). Its barcode is a (1 + epsilon)-multiplicative approximation of the Vietoris-Rips barcode (Theorem 5), from a complex of size linear in the number of points for data of bounded doubling dimension. (Sheehy 2013's epsilon is a different parameter: its factor is 1/(1 - 2 epsilon).) The edges are computed from all pairs, O(n^2), rather than by the paper's O(n log n) neighbour search: the complex to reduce is small, its construction is not.

==The construction==

Given a greedy permutation with insertion radii lambda_p (Infinity for the first point) and epsilon in (0, 1):

  • the ball of p at scale alpha has radius min(alpha, lambda_p (1 + epsilon) / epsilon);
  • it is empty from alpha > lambda_p (1 + epsilon)^2 / epsilon on (vanish(p)): no new simplex uses p after that, though nothing already present is removed (the filtration is the running union of the nerves);
  • an edge {p, q} is born at the smallest alpha at which the two balls meet (Algorithm 3, edgeBirth);
  • a simplex is born at the latest birth of its edges, if that is at most the earliest vanish of its vertices (Section 5.3), and never otherwise.

Algorithm 3 computes an edge's birth without the vanish check that Section 5.3 requires of every simplex (for epsilon = 1, lambda_p = 1, lambda_q = 10, d = 10 it gives 8, while p vanishes at 4); edgeBirth applies the check to edges too.

Units: the paper's alpha is a radius; every value here is doubled, so that values are diameters like every other Vietoris-Rips filtration (an unsparsified edge gets exactly its length).

maxFiltrationValue is always clamped to maxFiniteFiltrationValue, the largest finite edge birth: the enclosing radius is no bound here, and an unclamped Infinity threshold would admit simplices that should never appear.

The value of a simplex is not its diameter, so the Ripser engines do not apply; the naive, chunks and cohomology engines do.

open class SignedUnionFind[C](size: Int)(using fr: is[C, Field])

Union-find over 0 until size in which every element carries an orientation, a unit of the field C, relative to the root of its component. It is the bookkeeping behind the representatives of the dual union-find engines (FastCubicalHomologyEngine, FastAlphaHomologyEngine): an element is a top cell, a component a region of top cells, and the region's coherently oriented sum is sum of orientation(c) * c over its members.

Union-find over 0 until size in which every element carries an orientation, a unit of the field C, relative to the root of its component. It is the bookkeeping behind the representatives of the dual union-find engines (FastCubicalHomologyEngine, FastAlphaHomologyEngine): an element is a top cell, a component a region of top cells, and the region's coherently oriented sum is sum of orientation(c) * c over its members.

  • find compresses paths and composes orientations along them, so orientation(i) is amortised near-constant.
  • union(young, old, flip) hangs root young under root old, multiplying the whole young component's orientations by flip (a unit, ±1 in practice). It never touches the members.
  • The merges also form a forest that path compression does not change: members(root) walks the subtree of a root, which is frozen once that root has been merged away, and returns every member with its orientation relative to that root.

A merge therefore costs nearly constant time, and a representative costs time proportional to its region, paid only for the bars that are reported.

object TakensEmbedding

Sliding-window (Takens delay) embedding of a time series into a point cloud: the point at time t is the window (x_t, x_{t+delay}, ..., x_{t+(dimension-1) delay}). A periodic signal traces a closed curve in the window space, so Persistence(TakensEmbedding(signal, dimension = 2, delay = quarterPeriod)) shows the period as a long bar of degree 1; a quasi-periodic one traces a torus.

Sliding-window (Takens delay) embedding of a time series into a point cloud: the point at time t is the window (x_t, x_{t+delay}, ..., x_{t+(dimension-1) delay}). A periodic signal traces a closed curve in the window space, so Persistence(TakensEmbedding(signal, dimension = 2, delay = quarterPeriod)) shows the period as a long bar of degree 1; a quasi-periodic one traces a torus.

The dimension and delay decide what the embedding shows: too small a delay flattens the curve onto a line, too large a one folds it. delayByAutocorrelation gives a first guess for the delay.

object ToMATo

ToMATo, Topological Mode Analysis Tool (Chazal, Guibas, Oudot, Skraba, "Persistence-based clustering in Riemannian manifolds", J. ACM 60, 2013): clustering by the peaks of a density, where a peak counts only if it is persistent.

ToMATo, Topological Mode Analysis Tool (Chazal, Guibas, Oudot, Skraba, "Persistence-based clustering in Riemannian manifolds", J. ACM 60, 2013): clustering by the peaks of a density, where a peak counts only if it is persistent.

Take a function f (a density estimate: large at the centre of a cluster) on the vertices of a graph (which vertices are neighbours). Walk through the vertices from the highest value down. A vertex with no higher neighbour is a '''peak''' and starts a cluster; any other vertex joins the cluster of its highest neighbour, and if it also touches another cluster, the two merge when the lower of their peaks is less than tau above the vertex, that is, when the valley between them is shallower than tau. So tau is a depth: peaks that rise more than tau above every pass that joins them stay separate clusters.

The depths of all the valleys are the finite bars of the degree-0 persistent homology of f on the graph, which diagram returns; choose tau in a gap of that diagram, between the depths of the peaks you want and the depths of the noise (Plot.barcode(ToMATo.diagram(...)) shows it).

Bars are in the library's sublevel convention for a superlevel filtration: a peak of height h is born at -h, so a bar's persistence is the depth of its valley.
