open class VantagePointTree[V](elements: Seq[V], val distance: (V, V) => Double, val leafSize: Int = ...)

A vantage-point tree over elements: a static index for range and nearest-neighbour queries in any metric.

A vantage-point tree over elements: a static index for range and nearest-neighbour queries in any metric.

Each inner node holds one element (its vantage point) and splits the rest by distance to it, the nearer half to one child and the farther half to the other; the triangle inequality then lets a query skip a child without measuring its elements. Nodes with at most leafSize elements are scanned directly.

What a query returns does not depend on the tree's shape:

  • withinDistance(query, radius) is every element e with distance(query, e) &lt;= radius, the boundary included (the comparison is on the computed distance, so an element exactly at the radius is found), in the order of elements.
  • nearest(query, k) is the k elements nearest to query, nearest first, the first k of the stable sort of elements by distance: among elements at equal distance the one earlier in elements comes first. k larger than size returns all of them.

Both equal a linear scan whenever distance is a metric. Pruning compares distances with a relative slack of 1e-12, so the rounding of a computed metric (Euclidean distances violate the triangle inequality in the last bits) never hides an element. A distance that violates the triangle inequality by more than that (a correlation-derived dissimilarity, say) may make a query miss elements; use BruteForce for those.

The tree is built deterministically (a fixed pseudo-random choice of vantage points, a split at the median), is balanced whatever the data, and handles coincident elements: it builds in O(n log n) distance evaluations, a query costs O(log n) distance evaluations in low dimension. distance must be symmetric, non-negative and not NaN; infinite distances are allowed.

Type parameters

V

the element type, which is also the type of a query

Value parameters

distance

a metric on the elements

elements

the indexed elements; positions in this sequence are the indices the ...Indices queries return

leafSize

the largest number of elements scanned without further splitting (at least 1)

class WeightedGraph extends FiniteMetricSpace[Int]

A weighted undirected graph on the vertices 0 until n, held as sorted neighbour lists: n + 2 m numbers for m edges, where a distance matrix holds n^2. It is a metric space in the sense the Vietoris-Rips machinery needs: the distance of two vertices is 0 for the same vertex, the weight of the edge between them, and Infinity where there is none (the triangle inequality does not hold; this is the combinatorial reading, the flag complex of the listed edges). Persistence(graph) computes that flag complex with FlagComplex, without ever forming a matrix.

It is a metric space in the sense the Vietoris-Rips machinery needs: the distance of two vertices is 0 for the same vertex, the weight of the edge between them, and Infinity where there is none (the triangle inequality does not hold; this is the combinatorial reading, the flag complex of the listed edges). Persistence(graph) computes that flag complex with FlagComplex, without ever forming a matrix.

val graph = WeightedGraph(4, Seq((0, 1, 1.0), (1, 2, 1.5), (2, 3, 1.0), (3, 0, 2.0)))
Persistence(graph).dim(1)   // the square is a loop: born when its last edge enters, at 2.0, never filled

object ZigzagPersistence

Zigzag persistent homology: the homology of a sequence of complexes in which each is included in the next or the next in it, in either direction, as a barcode of intervals. A sequence K_0, K_1, ..., K_n is read in positions 0..n, and a bar [b, d) is a class that is in the homology of K_b, ..., K_{d-1} and in neither neighbour; the d of a class still there at K_n is infinite. With every arrow forward this is the ordinary barcode of a filtration with one cell, or one batch of cells, entering at each position.

Zigzag persistent homology: the homology of a sequence of complexes in which each is included in the next or the next in it, in either direction, as a barcode of intervals. A sequence K_0, K_1, ..., K_n is read in positions 0..n, and a bar [b, d) is a class that is in the homology of K_b, ..., K_{d-1} and in neither neighbour; the d of a class still there at K_n is infinite. With every arrow forward this is the ordinary barcode of a filtration with one cell, or one batch of cells, entering at each position.

val steps = Seq(Add(Simplex(0)), Add(Simplex(1)), Add(Simplex(0, 1)), Remove(Simplex(0, 1)))
val diagram = ZigzagPersistence(steps)

The input is a list of ZigzagSteps (apply), a list of complexes each included in the next or the next in it (ofComplexes), with the union or the intersection of consecutive complexes put between them when they are not (Link.Union, as for a time-varying point cloud). The result is an ordinary PersistenceDiagram: its bars have a representative, a cycle in the complex at the bar's birth, and every tool for diagrams applies.

The decomposition is made from left to right, one arrow at a time, on the homology of the complexes (Carlsson and de Silva): a basis of the homology at the current position, each class with its birth, in an order that the arrows decide (a class born by an arrow forward goes last, one born in the kernel of an arrow backward goes first). An arrow forward reduces the images of the classes in that order and the classes that vanish end. An arrow backward puts the classes of the smaller complex in the basis of the current homology, adapted to the order, and the classes outside its image end. Only the dimensions an arrow touches are recomputed, by sparse elimination on the boundary matrices of the larger complex of the arrow: each arrow costs a reduction of those, so the method is meant for sequences of up to a few thousand cells in the dimensions that change.

An elementary cube: a product I_1 x ... x I_n of intervals, each a point [a, a] or a unit interval [a, a+1]. Its dimension is the number of unit intervals; n, the ambient dimension, is the same for every cube of a complex.

Coordinates are doubled (Kaczynski, Mischaikow, Mrozek, ''Computational Homology''): [a, a] is 2a and [a, a+1] is 2a + 1, so a cube is one Vector[Int] (with structural equality, which the reductions rely on).

Cube is OrderedCell instance -- mirrors Simplex.scala's simplexIsOrderedCell parameterized-given pattern exactly, so a stream can inject its own filtration-aware ordering the same way EnumeratingCofaceSimplexStream etc. do for Simplex[Int].

Boundary formula (Kaczynski-Mischaikow-Mrozek's standard cubical boundary operator, matching exactly what was asked for: "collapse each unit interval to a degenerate interval both ways, opposite signs, once per unit- interval factor"): for a cube with non-degenerate axes at positions p_1 &lt; p_2 &lt; ... &lt; p_d (0-indexed into the coordinate vector, d = the cube's own dimension), the boundary is

sum_{l=1}^{d} (-1)^(l-1) * (cube with axis p_l collapsed to its UPPER endpoint - cube with axis p_l collapsed to its LOWER endpoint)

i.e. the sign alternates over the RANK of the axis among non-degenerate axes (l, 0-indexed as rank below), not over its raw position in the coordinate vector -- using the raw position instead is a real, easy-to-make sign bug that breaks d(d(x)) = 0 as soon as a cube has a degenerate axis interleaved among its non-degenerate ones. Verified by CubicalSpec's dd=0 property test over a signed field (F3), not just F2 -- F2 cannot distinguish a correct alternating sign from a constant one, since -1 = 1 there.
